messages.author: 9dd9ea947d797759
messages.subject: Stan code development and consulting needed
parts:
Does anyone on the Stan development team do consulting?

I'm likely to have some salary money left over on a grant, because my postdoc got a fellowship. To finish what we wanted to do, we need to fit a multivariate linear stochastic differential equation time series model with multinomial observation error in Stan. We're working with stochastic differential equations that have explicit solutions. I haven't yet written down exactly what the solutions are, but they will definitely involve matrix exponentials. If I've understood the current state of Stan correctly, matrix exponentials aren't yet implemented, but could be with a bit of work. We'd also need the models coded efficiently in Stan (I could only code them very inefficiently). Obviously, coauthorship on the resulting paper would be part of the deal.

Matt

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Stan code development and consulting needed
parts:
On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 1:34:13 PM UTC-4, Matthew Spencer wrote:
If I've understood the current state of Stan correctly, matrix exponentials aren't yet implemented, but could be with a bit of work.

A bit would be an understatement since
  • Eigen wouldn't take my patch to make the pseudo-eigendecomposition only use real operations internally ( http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/bz/show_bug.cgi?id=1029 )
  • And we're not particularly close to supporting complex numbers ( https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/123 )
  • And the unsupported matrix exponential function that is already in Eigen doesn't support custom scalar types ( http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/unsupported/group__MatrixFunctions__Module.html )
  • So you would have autodiff the matrix exponential function analytically ( https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=7538355619694802842&hl=en&as_sdt=1,33 ), which that paper claims "can be obtained by combining the earlier results for the matrix inverse product and polynomial (page 7)"
  • But we don't exactly understand that paper
  • And even if we did, the whole thing might well be numerically unstable.

Ben

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan code development and consulting needed
parts:
The algorithm is indeed hairy, and coding it in Stan is really
stretching the limits of the language, but then one gets the
derivative automatically.

My understanding is that Stan can't just grab expm from an
existing library, because it also need the Jacobian --- is this
correct, or are there other obstacles/requirements (licensing
etc)?

I did a bit of reading about the Jacobian of the matrix
exponential. Higham's "Functions of Matrices" mentions the
derivative in Section 10.6, and suggests that there is a nice
duality between the matrix exponential and its Frechet derivative
(you can use expm on a special block matrix to get the derivative
at the same time). But this is inefficient and there are two
special algorithms.

So the question is this: would a C++ function which, for a given
matrix A, computes expm(A) and its Jacobian, be sufficient for
solving this problem?

Al-Mohy's thesis is about the derivative too, but I don't have
time to read it right now.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan code development and consulting needed
parts:
Jeff - I've written a couple of matrix exponential variants within STAN. I guess it's much slower than an ideal solution would be, but still works... here is the code for the functions. expmt is the taylor expansion approach (currently set to 50 iterations) while expmp uses pade approximants and is based on the R function expm.Higham08. The pade approach is more efficient and stable, but I couldn't think of a lazy way to incorporate the necessary matrix / vector of values so just put it in as data using my wrapper function for continuous time models. If you want to chat about it a bit more you're welcome to get in touch.

functions{

real factorial(int m);
real factorial(int m) {
      if (m == 0)
      return 1;
      else
      return (m * factorial(m-1));
}


matrix matrix_pow(matrix a, real n);
matrix matrix_pow(matrix a, real n) {
  if (n == 0){
  return diag_matrix(rep_vector(1, rows(a)));
}
  else
  return a * matrix_pow(a, n - 1);
}


matrix expmt(matrix mat, real t){
matrix[rows(mat),rows(mat)] out;
out<-diag_matrix(rep_vector(1.0, rows(mat)));
for(i in 1:50){
out<-out+ matrix_pow(mat,i) * t^i /factorial(i);
}
return out;
}




matrix expmp(matrix A, matrix padeC, vector padeCbig){
  int n;
real nA;
real colsum;
int l;
matrix[4,10] C;
vector[4] t;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] I;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] P;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] U;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] V;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] X;

vector[14] Cbig;
real s;
real si;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] B;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] B2;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] B4;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] B6;
matrix[rows(A),rows(A)] A2;

si <- 0;
C <- padeC;
Cbig <- padeCbig;

n <-rows(A);
if(n != cols(A)) print("expmp: Matrix not square!")

if (n <= 1) X <- exp(A);
else{

// nA <- Matrix::norm(A, "1")
nA <- 0;
for(coli in 1:n){
colsum<-0;
for(rowi in 1:n){
colsum<-colsum+fabs(A[rowi,coli]);
}
if(colsum > nA) nA <- colsum;
}

I <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(1,n));
if (nA <= 2.1) {
t[1] <- 0.015; t[2]<- 0.25; t[3]<- 0.95; t[4]<- 2.1;

//l <- which.max(nA <= t)
for(ti in 1:4){
if(l==0){
if(nA <= t[ti]) l <- ti;
}
}

A2 <- A * A;
P <- I;
U <- C[l, 2] * I;
V <- C[l, 1] * I;
for (k in 1:l) {
P <- P * A2;
U <- U + C[l, (2 * k) + 2] * P;
V <- V + C[l, (2 * k) + 1] * P;
}
U <- A * U;
X <- inverse(V - U) * (V + U);
}

else {
s <- log2(nA/5.4);
B <- A;
if (s > 0) {
s <- ceil(s);
B <- B/(2^s);
}

B2 <- B * B;
B4 <- B2 * B2;
B6 <- B2*B4;
U <- B*(B6*(Cbig[14] * B6 + Cbig[12] * B4 + Cbig[10] * B2) + Cbig[8] * B6 + Cbig[6] * B4 + Cbig[4] * B2 + Cbig[2] * I);
V <- B6*(Cbig[13] * B6 + Cbig[11] * B4 + Cbig[9] * B2) + Cbig[7] * B6 + Cbig[5] * B4 + Cbig[3] * B2 + Cbig[1] * I;
X <- inverse(V - U) * (V + U);

if (s > 0) {
while (si < s){
si <- si + 1;
X <- X * X;
}
}
}

}
return X;
  }

  for (i in 1:m){

  }
  }
